en: Jātaka: The Book of the Seven Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Cocks (Kukkuvagga)
1. The Kukkujātaka:
“The central nave rises one and a half cubits; eight spans surround it.”
“That *siṃsapā* tree is made of heartwood, without pith;
standing where it is, it does not fall over.
“Those thirty [trees] are made of heartwood, yet they are not straight.”
The rafters, having been arranged all around, stand level;
well-supported by them and pressed firmly together,
they remain level and do not collapse from above.
In this way, a wise man, well-supported by firm friends who are incorruptible, pure,
and sagacious, does not fall away from prosperity.
The rafters bear the weight, while the central pillar is the bearer of the load.
Just as a caravan leader, even without tasting it himself, makes the bitter bell fruit [bitter]; so too does the teacher.
O King, by collecting [the right ingredients], one makes it delicious;
by removing the bodily impurities, one makes it unpalatable.
In this same way, the wise man acts within villages and market towns.
Gathering royal wealth without violence,
acting in accordance with the Dhamma,
he would bring about prosperity without harming others.
Just as a lotus born in lotus ponds has its roots white and arises from pure water,
and just as a red lotus is scorched by the heat of the sun's rays;
Neither mud, nor dust, nor water stains him. Even so,
one who is pure in conventional conduct, free from violence, whose actions are purified, and who has abandoned evil— his fame spreads abroad.
Such a person is not defiled by the taints of karma,
just as a lotus born in lotus ponds is not soiled.
Thus ends the first Jātaka, the Kukkujātaka.
